Chapter Six: Imperfection, Folly, and the Art of Being Ordinary.
Have you ever felt that quiet relief when you finally realize—perfection isn’t just impossible, it’s actually not even necessary? Most of us spend years chasing this ideal, always trying to be flawless at work, in our relationships, maybe even in our own thoughts.
The pressure builds. Every small mistake suddenly feels huge, and our shortcomings turn into sources of shame. But what if imperfection isn’t a flaw at all? What if it’s actually just part of being human?
Picture someone who always tries to say the right thing, never wants to offend, and aims to look composed no matter what. That kind of effort gets exhausting, right? And sooner or later, there’s a slip—a careless word, a forgotten promise, maybe just a moment of impatience. But you know what? The world doesn’t end. Sometimes, those little stumbles even bring out laughter, more understanding, or a deeper connection with others.
Montaigne, the French philosopher, loved telling stories about regular people making everyday mistakes. Think of a merchant who miscalculates and loses some money, a parent who loses their temper, or a friend who forgets an important date. Those moments can sting, but they also show us something important: everyone’s fallible. And the more we accept that, the lighter life starts to feel.
There’s real wisdom in embracing a bit of folly—not the reckless kind that hurts others, but that gentle, human foolishness that comes from trying, failing, and then trying again. It’s being able to laugh at yourself, admit when you just don’t get something, and let go of needing to always be right.
Imagine this: it’s a lazy afternoon, and a group of neighbors gathers for a meal. The conversation drifts from politics to family stories, and pretty soon, someone shares an embarrassing mishap from their youth. Laughter ripples around the table, and the stories just keep coming—everyone takes a turn sharing their own blunders and misunderstandings. In that moment, all the pressure to seem perfect just melts away, replaced by a real sense of belonging.
If you think about it, most of us are drawn to people who are comfortable with their own imperfections. There’s a special warmth in someone who can shrug off a mistake, offer a sincere apology, and then move on. It reminds us that life isn’t a performance—it’s about sharing the experience, together.
The art of being ordinary doesn’t mean settling for less. It’s about finding real contentment in the everyday. It’s noticing those small pleasures—a delicious meal, a kind word, a peaceful evening—and letting go of the urge to impress. It’s about accepting that we’re all works in progress, and that true growth doesn’t come from denying our flaws, but from living honestly with them.
